subject: Archaeology
title: Cuneiform: The First Writing System
description: A quick, practical guide to Cuneiform: The First Writing System.

hook.text: The oldest writing on earth was pressed into wet clay with a reed stylus. Over 500,000 tablets have survived.

buildup.text: Cuneiform started as pictures around 3400 BCE and evolved into abstract wedge-shaped marks representing sounds.

discovery.text: Henry Rawlinson deciphered cuneiform in the 1840s using a trilingual inscription carved high on a cliff at Behistun.

twist.text: Cuneiform was used by Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians, Assyrians, Hittites, and even Persians.

climax.text: AI is now being used to read damaged tablets. Machine learning can fill in broken signs that humans struggle to read.

punchline.text: They wrote on mud with a stick. Five hundred thousand of those notes survived.

quiz.question: How was cuneiform deciphered?
options: A bilingual dictionary was found in a sealed library in Babylon
Henry Rawlinson used a trilingual inscription carved on a cliff at Behistun
Scholars compared it to Egyptian hieroglyphs using the Rosetta Stone

details.summary: Cuneiform writing used wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay tablets. Invented around 3200 BCE in Sumer, it evolved from pictographs into an abstract script used across Mesopotamia for over three thousand years to record everything from grain tallies to epic poetry.
details.whyItMatters: Cuneiform is humanity's first writing system. Its decipherment unlocked thousands of years of forgotten history, literature, and law, transforming our understanding of ancient civilizations.
takeaways: Cuneiform used wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay tablets
It evolved from pictographic to abstract over centuries
The system served Mesopotamian cultures for over 3,000 years

faq.question: How was cuneiform deciphered?
faq.answer: Henry Rawlinson copied inscriptions from the Behistun cliff in Iran, which featured the same text in Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian cuneiform. By cracking Old Persian first, scholars worked backward to unlock Babylonian cuneiform in the 1850s.

faq.question: How many cuneiform tablets survive today?
faq.answer: Roughly half a million tablets are held in museums worldwide, and many more remain unexcavated. Because clay tablets survive fire and burial well, cuneiform left an enormous written record compared to civilizations that wrote on perishable materials.
